recent_works.title: The New Is Old Again
recent_works.abstract: This chapter outlines the pattern and structure of NATO and Russian exercises between 2014 and 2018, setting them in the context of the increasingly strained relationship between the two actors. Despite media emphasis on size, Russia often constructed exercises below CSBM thresholds, limiting formal observation. NATO exercises increased after 2014, reversing Cold War patterns by conducting fewer extremely large-scale exercises than Russia but frequently conducting smaller-scale exercises. Undermining efforts to use exercises for nuanced signalling, NATO members’ national exercises occurred in parallel with official NATO exercises but lacked centralized planning.

recent_works.title: The Missing Span
recent_works.abstract: This chapter provides an analysis of the theory and reality of confidence-building in Europe, drawing on ideas of vulnerability as part of trust-building and the meaning of “confidence”. While C(S)BMs may raise short-term confidence in the benign intent of an exercising force, this is based on reconfiguring the costs of a surprise attack, rather than developing a belief that the exercising party would not attack even if the costs were low. In the medium term, C(S)BMs enhancing confidence in the low likelihood of attack again stemmed from the ability to measure others’ capability. That is, the possibility that the potential attacker overestimates its chances of winning diminishes, reducing the likelihood of escalation. Mutual adherence to the C(S)BMs, therefore, could develop confidence that others will not attack in the short and medium term by indicating the balance of capability, but does not generate a trusting relationship. This was highlighted by the introduction of “Security” into Confidence-Building, which indicated a new understanding of the intent of the regime. recent_works.title: The Stockholm Document
recent_works.abstract: This chapter provides an analysis of the updated CBMs included in the Stockholm Document and the overt introduction of “Security” into Confidence-Building Measures to create “Confidence- and Security-Building Measures”. As with the previous chapter, this focuses on the intended effect of the Stockholm Document, emphasizing the way in which the regime was intended to move beyond the Helsinki Final Act. This required a shift from using CBMs to ensure that there could not be a surprise attack founded in an exercise, to using the observation of exercises to generate an accurate interpretation of the medium-term intent of another actor. The chapter then covers the difference in priorities of NATO and the Soviet Union, highlighting the greater willingness of NATO to institutionalize transparency and the Soviet priority of “declaratory measures”. The analysis of archival documents also demonstrates the competitive nature of the negotiations and the NATO perception of Soviet “duplicity” in their negotiating position.

recent_works.title: Through the Looking Glass
recent_works.abstract: This chapter assesses NATO and Soviet responses to others’ exercises and the concerns that were particularly significant in re-shaping the perception of threat. Ultimately, while NATO remained concerned about the potential for an exercise to turn into offensive action, it was the breach of the C(S)BM regime that led most directly to NATO perceiving a threat from Soviet exercises. In breaking the rules, the Soviet Union undermined NATO&s;s efforts to build security through mutually agreed rules and NATO felt itself in a threateningly unpredictable environment. The Soviet Union, with a less socially grounded commitment to openness and rule-following, usually followed the letter of rules and used the transparency generated by the C(S)BM regime where it saw an advantage, but did not put the regime at the centre of their approach to security. Soviet concerns around exercises focused on NATO&s;s ability to gather forces in Europe. Large-scale exercises were considered threatening, and Soviet reaction to Able Archer 83 , as well as the scenario in Druzhba 85 , demonstrates that they viewed the possibility of NATO transforming an exercise into offensive action as realistic.
